name: AI and learning
statements: b0
Jason Gibson, a history professor at Alcorn State University, embedded a hidden instruction in his midterm exam that instructed students to place the word Madagascar in their responses.
b1
New York City's AI ban affects approximately 600,000 public school students, nearly two-thirds of the district's total enrollment.
b2
China requires at least eight hours of AI instruction per year in schools.
b3
AI in schools is being deployed by districts with limited evidence about its educational impact or comprehensive policies.
b4
Regular use of the Amira AI reading program contributes to measurable improvements in students' reading abilities.
b5
Restricting or banning children's access to AI in school will hold them back from skills they will need in the future.
b6
Banning generative AI for young students is justified to protect their critical thinking abilities and teacher-student relationships.
b7
School districts should establish clear, evidence-based policies before deploying AI tools in classrooms.
b8
New York City announced a one-year moratorium banning generative AI use for public school students from prekindergarten through eighth grade.
b9
At Brown University, 40 of 86 students in the economics course received perfect or nearly perfect scores on the midterm exam.
New York City's policy caps screentime on individual devices at 30 minutes for third through fifth grade students.
The AI-assisted cheating uncovered in Professor Roberto Serrano's take-home midterm at Brown University is one of the largest such scandals in Ivy League history.
Embedding a hidden instruction inside an AI exam prompt causes students who copy the prompt into AI tools to unknowingly reveal that they did not write the response themselves.
AI will fundamentally reshape the future of education.
AI tools that help identify learning disabilities like dyslexia provide valuable support that improves student outcomes.
Educators should administer exams in person rather than as take-home assignments to prevent AI-assisted cheating.
The Southeast Delco School District in Delaware County implemented Amira, an AI-powered literacy tool, as a pilot program in the 2024-2025 school year.
A study of 27,000 students in China found that homework scores rose by 18 percent after adopting generative AI.
New York City's policy requires students in preschool through second grade to largely lose access to individual devices in class.
Students using AI to complete homework without adequate learning is a significant problem in K-12 and higher education.
Widespread generative AI use by students is eroding their critical thinking abilities.
Student exam performance will continue to decline in districts where AI is permitted for homework completion without restrictions.
Students who use AI to cheat on assignments deserve academic consequences.
Schools should limit student screentime on devices to protect their learning and development.
